\chapter{What You Think Of It}
\label{ch:ml-opinion}
\hlchaptermodality{89}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that something is good or bad, and say that I think so.}

From cold: the ending that lets a quality stand alone, the negative the book had been missing, and the opinion frame that needed no new grammar.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[nallathŭ]{\ml{നല്ലത്} (nallathŭ) — a good one}

\label{lesson:ML-C89-nallathu}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{good}. Then say where it has to stand, and what it needs after it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a quality with nothing to lean on}]
\textbf{\ml{നല്ല}} has always needed a noun to sit in front of. You can say \emph{a good book} and you cannot say \textbf{the good one} — there is nothing for the quality to lean on.

\textbf{-\ml{അത്} fixes that.} Put it on the end of a quality and the quality becomes a thing:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{നല്ല}} & good — needs a noun after it \\
\textbf{\ml{നല്ലത്}} & \textbf{a good one}, a good thing — stands alone \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

And look at what that ending is. \textbf{\ml{അത്}} is the word for \emph{that}, which you have had since the pointing chapter. \textbf{\ml{നല്ലത്}} is \emph{the that-which-is-good} — the sense fits the shape exactly.

\textbf{This works on every quality the book has given you}, and that is the reason it is worth a lesson rather than a footnote:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{വലിയ}} $\to$ \textbf{\ml{വലിയത്}} & a big one \\
\textbf{\ml{ചെറിയ}} $\to$ \textbf{\ml{ചെറിയത്}} & a small one \\
\textbf{\ml{പുതിയ}} $\to$ \textbf{\ml{പുതിയത്}} & a new one \\
\textbf{\ml{പഴയ}} $\to$ \textbf{\ml{പഴയത്}} & an old one \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Five qualities, one ending, and \textbf{no exceptions among them.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nalla}, then \emph{nallathŭ}
  \item which of the two can stand without a noun after it
  \item the word for \emph{that}, and where you can see it in \emph{nallathŭ}
  \item \emph{valiyathŭ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{-\ml{അത്}} do to a quality? (\textbf{Turns it into a thing}.) What ordinary word is that ending? (\emph{\textbf{that}}.) And how many of your qualities does it work on? (\textbf{All of them}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mōśaṁ]{\ml{മോശം} (mōśaṁ) — bad}

\label{lesson:ML-C89-mosham}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{a good one}. Then notice what you still cannot say about anything at all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{മോശം}}
\textbf{\ml{മോശം}} — \emph{mōśaṁ} — bad, poor.

\textbf{The book has given you five qualities and not one of them is negative.} A thing could be good, big, small, new or old, and there was no way to say it was \textbf{bad} — which is half of every opinion anybody has ever offered.

Put it with the \emph{is} word you have had since the second chapter:

\textbf{\ml{മോശമാണ്}} — \emph{mōśamāṇŭ} — it is bad.

Notice the join. \textbf{\ml{മോശം}} ends in the \textbf{\ml{ം}}, and when \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} follows it that \textbf{\ml{ം}} is written \textbf{\ml{മ}}. You have seen this book change a word's shape before something else attaches; this is the same habit in a smaller place.

The partner sentence is built the same way, from the word you learned a moment ago: \textbf{\ml{നല്ലതാണ്}} — \emph{nallathāṇŭ} — it is good.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mōśaṁ}
  \item \emph{mōśamāṇŭ}
  \item what happened to the \textbf{\ml{ം}} when the \emph{is} word arrived
  \item \emph{nallathāṇŭ}, then \emph{mōśamāṇŭ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{mōśaṁ} mean? (\textbf{Bad}.) How do you say \emph{it is bad}? (\emph{\textbf{mōśamāṇŭ}}.) And how was the \textbf{\ml{ം}} written once \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} followed? (\textbf{\ml{മ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nallathāṇŭ ennŭ ñān cintikkunnu]{\ml{നല്ലതാണ്} \ml{എന്ന്} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{ചിന്തിക്കുന്നു} — I think it is good}

\label{lesson:ML-C89-opinion}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{it is bad}. Then say the marker that turns any sentence into something you can report.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: nothing new is needed}]
An opinion is \textbf{a sentence with your own judgement wrapped around it}, and you now have both halves.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{അത്} \ml{നല്ലതാണ്} \ml{എന്ന്} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{ചിന്തിക്കുന്നു}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{atŭ nallathāṇŭ ennŭ ñān cintikkunnu} — \textbf{I think it is good.}
\end{quote}

Take it apart and \textbf{every piece is already yours}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{where it came from} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{അത്} \ml{നല്ലതാണ്}} & this chapter — \emph{it is good} \\
\textbf{\ml{എന്ന്}} & the quoting marker \\
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{ചിന്തിക്കുന്നു}} & the thinking verb, already paired with that marker \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The quoting chapter did the hard part.} It showed that the marker takes whatever sentence you can build and hands it to a verb of saying, thinking, knowing or asking — so an opinion needed \textbf{no new grammar at all}, only something worth having an opinion about.

Swap the inner sentence and the frame does not move:

\textbf{\ml{അത്} \ml{മോശമാണ്} \ml{എന്ന്} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{ചിന്തിക്കുന്നു}} — I think it is bad.

\textbf{This is what a well-built system looks like from the inside.} Two vocabulary words arrived, and a whole function — giving an opinion — came with them, because the machinery was already in place and waiting for something to carry.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{atŭ nallathāṇŭ}
  \item the whole opinion — \emph{atŭ nallathāṇŭ ennŭ ñān cintikkunnu}
  \item the same sentence with \emph{bad} instead
  \item which part of the opinion is new to this chapter
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What wraps your judgement around a sentence? (\textbf{\ml{എന്ന്} and a thinking verb}.) How much new grammar did the opinion need? (\textbf{None}.) And what changes when the opinion does? (\textbf{Only the inner sentence}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[abhipraayam enna ōrmma]{(what you think of it) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R89-opinion-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{a good one}, then say \emph{bad}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a quality standing on its own}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{നല്ല}} & good — needs a noun after it \\
\textbf{\ml{നല്ലത്}} & \textbf{a good one} — stands alone \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{-\ml{അത്}} is the word for \emph{that}, and \textbf{\ml{നല്ലത്}} is \emph{the that-which-is-good}. The sense fits the shape, and the ending works on \textbf{every quality the book has given you} — \emph{valiyathŭ}, \emph{ceṟiyathŭ}, \emph{puthiyathŭ}, \emph{paḻayathŭ} — with no exceptions among them.

\textbf{\ml{മോശം}} filled the other hole. Five qualities and not one of them negative meant half of every opinion was unsayable. Before the \emph{is} word, its \textbf{\ml{ം}} becomes \textbf{\ml{മ}}: \textbf{\ml{മോശമാണ്}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
An opinion, out of parts that were already lying about.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{അത്} \ml{നല്ലതാണ്} \ml{എന്ന്} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{ചിന്തിക്കുന്നു}.} — I think it is good.
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{new?} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{അത്} \ml{നല്ലതാണ്}} & the two words of this chapter \\
\textbf{\ml{എന്ന്}} & \textbf{no} — the quoting marker \\
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{ചിന്തിക്കുന്നു}} & \textbf{no} — already paired with that marker \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The quoting chapter did the hard part} when it showed the marker takes any sentence you can build and hands it to a verb of saying, thinking, knowing or asking. So this chapter added \textbf{two vocabulary words and no grammar}, and a whole function arrived with them.

That is worth noticing about how this book is built: \textbf{machinery is often in place before there is anything worth carrying with it}, and the chapter that finally uses it can be very small.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nallathŭ}, then \emph{valiyathŭ}
  \item \emph{mōśamāṇŭ}
  \item the whole opinion, with \emph{good}
  \item the same opinion, with \emph{bad}
  \item which parts of it this chapter actually taught you
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{-\ml{അത്}} do to a quality? (\textbf{Makes it a thing that can stand alone}.) What is \emph{bad}? (\emph{\textbf{mōśaṁ}}.) And how much new grammar did the opinion need? (\textbf{None.})
\end{tcolorbox}
